claim: Drosophila larvae adjust the frequency of locomotion mostly by varying the time between consecutive contraction waves.
source: We find that larvae adjust the frequency of locomotion mostly by varying the time between consecutive contraction waves, reminiscent of limbed locomotion.
evidence: Supported by kinematic analysis data presented in Figure 1 showing correlation between interwave phase duration and locomotion speed.

claim: The lateral transverse (LT) muscles co-contract in all segments during the interwave phase.
source: A specific set of muscles, the lateral transverse (LT) muscles, co-contract in all segments during this phase, the duration of which sets the duration of the interwave phase.
evidence: Supported by side-view imaging data showing synchronous LT muscle contractions across segments A2-A7 during the interwave phase (Figure 1K, Figure 1—figure supplement 1G').

claim: The duration of the LT muscle contractions sets the duration of the interwave phase.
source: A specific set of muscles, the lateral transverse (LT) muscles, co-contract in all segments during this phase, the duration of which sets the duration of the interwave phase.
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis showing strong correlation (r = 0.89) between LT2 muscle contraction duration and interwave phase duration (Figure 1L).

claim: GABAergic interneuron A26f is a premotor neuron that exhibits segmentally synchronized activity.
source: We identify two types of GABAergic interneurons in the LT neural network, premotor neuron A26f and its presynaptic partner A31c, which exhibit segmentally synchronized activity and control locomotor frequency by setting the amplitude and duration of LT muscle contractions.
evidence: Supported by calcium imaging showing synchronized activity of A26f neurons across segments (Figure 4C-E) and immunostaining showing GABAergic identity (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).

claim: GABAergic interneuron A31c is presynaptic to A26f and exhibits segmentally synchronized activity.
source: We identify two types of GABAergic interneurons in the LT neural network, premotor neuron A26f and its presynaptic partner A31c, which exhibit segmentally synchronized activity and control locomotor frequency by setting the amplitude and duration of LT muscle contractions.
evidence: Supported by EM connectomics showing A31c-A26f connectivity (Figure 3D), trans-Tango tracing (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C and D), calcium imaging showing synchronized activity (Figure 2C-E), and immunostaining showing GABAergic identity (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).

claim: A26f and A31c neurons control locomotor frequency by setting the amplitude and duration of LT muscle contractions.
source: We identify two types of GABAergic interneurons in the LT neural network, premotor neuron A26f and its presynaptic partner A31c, which exhibit segmentally synchronized activity and control locomotor frequency by setting the amplitude and duration of LT muscle contractions.
evidence: Supported by optogenetic manipulation experiments showing that activation/inhibition of A26f and A31c affects LT muscle contraction amplitude (Figures 5, 6) and locomotor frequency (Figure 7).

claim: Locomotion speed in freely crawling third-instar larvae ranges from 0.35 to 1.23 mm/s.
source: Larvae crawled at varying speeds even within the same environmental conditions such as temperature (Figure 1D and E, 0.35–1.23 mm/s, n = 18 larvae).
evidence: Supported by direct measurement from top-view crawling assay data.

claim: Locomotion speed correlates more strongly with stride frequency than with stride length in freely crawling larvae.
source: We found that the locomotion speed in these freely crawling animals also correlated with stride frequency more so than stride length, consistent with a previous report (Heckscher et al., 2012; Figure 1E).
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis from top-view crawling data (Figure 1D, E) and cited previous work (Heckscher et al., 2012).

claim: The interwave phase is more strongly correlated with crawling speed than the wave phase.
source: We found that both the interwave phase and the wave phase are correlated with crawling speed (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C–C'; Pearson correlation coefficient: the wave phase vs. speed r = –0.62, the interwave phase vs. speed r = –0.74).
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis showing r = -0.74 for interwave phase vs. speed and r = -0.62 for wave phase vs. speed.

claim: The duty factor of the interwave phase decreases with speed.
source: indeed, the duty factor of the interwave phase, which is given by the ratio of the interwave phase duration to stride duration, decreased with speed (Figure 1I; linear regression coefficient = –0.47, r2 = 0.55) and was reduced to zero at the faster speeds.
evidence: Supported by regression analysis of top-view crawling data showing linear regression coefficient = -0.47.

claim: The interwave phase is correlated more strongly with stride duration than the wave phase.
source: Both are correlated with stride duration, with the interwave phase correlated more strongly than the wave phase (interwave phase r = 0.86, wave phase r = 0.56, p<0.0001).
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis showing r = 0.86 for interwave phase and r = 0.56 for wave phase with stride duration.

claim: As stride duration decreases, the interwave phase shortens while the wave duration stays relatively constant.
source: What becomes clear from this analysis is that as the stride duration decreases, the interwave phase shortens while the wave duration stays more or less constant; when the interwave duration becomes minimal, further decreases in stride duration are accompanied by decreases in wave duration.
evidence: Supported by analysis of phase durations as a function of stride duration (Figure 1—figure supplement 1F and F').

claim: Longitudinal muscles exhibit propagation from the posterior segment to the anterior during forward crawling.
source: first, consistent with a previous study (Heckscher et al., 2012), longitudinal muscles exhibited propagation from the posterior segment to the anterior in forward crawling (Figure 1L and Figure 1—figure supplement 1G').
evidence: Supported by side-view muscle imaging data and cited previous work (Heckscher et al., 2012).

claim: LT2 transverse muscles show synchronous contractions across abdominal segments A2-A7.
source: Second, the LT2 transverse muscles only showed synchronous contractions across abdominal segments A2-A7 (Figure 1K and Figure 1—figure supplement 1G'), in contrast to the earlier report (Heckscher et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by side-view muscle imaging data showing synchronous activity patterns.

claim: Transverse muscles contract exclusively during the interwave phase.
source: Furthermore, while most longitudinal muscles were contracting during peristaltic waves, the transverse muscles contracted exclusively during the interwave phase (Figure 1—figure supplement 1G').
evidence: Supported by temporal analysis of muscle contraction dynamics from side-view imaging.

claim: The duration of the interwave phase has a high correlation with the contraction duration of transverse muscles (r = 0.89).
source: While the duration of the wave phase was not strongly correlated, the duration of the interwave phase had a high correlation with the contraction duration of transverse muscles (wave phase r = 0.20, interwave phase r = 0.89, p<0.0001; the Pearson correlation coefficient, Figure 1L and M).
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis of muscle contraction duration and locomotor phase durations.

claim: The contraction duration of transverse muscles is correlated with crawling speed (r = -0.59).
source: We therefore plotted the duration of transverse muscle contractions against crawling speed (Figure 1N) and found that they were indeed correlated (r = –0.59).
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis between LT muscle contraction duration and speed.

claim: A31c neurons are GABAergic.
source: Using immunohistochemistry, we found that A31c neurons are GABAergic (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data showing GABA expression in A31c neurons.

claim: A31c neurons exhibit burst-like coactivation across all abdominal segments at the initiation of forward locomotion.
source: At the initiation of forward locomotion, all abdominal A31c neurons show burst-like coactivation preceding the FW (Figure 2C and D).
evidence: Supported by dual-color calcium imaging data in isolated CNS preparations.

claim: A31c neurons exhibit synchronous multi-segmental activity during the interwave phase.
source: To sum, these results show that A31c neurons exhibit synchronous multi-segmental activity during the interwave phase.
evidence: Supported by calcium imaging showing near-zero intersegmental lag during interwave phase (Figure 2E).

claim: The subesophageal descending neuron cell type S10 provides a significant plurality of the synaptic input to A31c neurons.
source: The same subesophageal descending neuron cell type (here labeled 'S10') provides a significant plurality of the synaptic input.
evidence: Supported by EM connectomics reconstruction and analysis of A31c synaptic partners (Figure 3D).

claim: A26f neurons are among the top three postsynaptic partners of A31c neurons in both anterior and posterior segments.
source: Among postsynaptic targets, we found that just one cell type is consistent between segments A2-A3 and A7-A8: A26f neurons, which are among their top three postsynaptic partners (Figure 3D).
evidence: Supported by EM connectomics analysis of A31c postsynaptic partners.

claim: A26f neurons strongly innervate transverse motor neurons.
source: Interestingly, it has previously been reported that A26f strongly innervates the transverse motor neurons (Zarin et al., 2019; Zwart et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by cited previous work (Zarin et al., 2019; Zwart et al., 2016).

claim: A26f neurons are GABAergic.
source: We found that A26f neurons are GABAergic (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data showing GABA expression in A26f neurons.

claim: A26f neurons are not corazoninergic.
source: However, a comparison of the morphology of A26f neurons with confirmed corazoninergic neurons (Santos et al., 2007) and the absence of peptidergic dense core vesicles in A26f neurons in the EM connectomics dataset suggest that A26f neurons are not corazoninergic.
evidence: Supported by morphological comparison with confirmed corazoninergic neurons and EM analysis showing absence of dense core vesicles.

claim: A26f neurons form inhibitory synapses onto motor neurons innervating LT muscles in multiple neuromeres.
source: A26f neurons form inhibitory synapses onto MNs innervating LT muscles in multiple neuromeres, which suggests the potential of A26f neurons to control the activity of LT muscles broadly in multiple segments.
evidence: Supported by EM connectomics analysis showing synaptic connections and GABAergic identity of A26f.

claim: A26f neurons show synchronized activity that mostly occurs before the fictive peristaltic wave progresses anteriorly from segment A4.
source: Unlike most neurons, which show fictive wave-like activity (Lemon et al., 2015), the A26f neurons we could image with this line only showed synchronized activity, which mostly occurred before the fictive peristaltic wave progressed anteriorly from segment A4 (Figure 4C and D).
evidence: Supported by dual-color calcium imaging data in isolated CNS preparations.

claim: A26f activity overlaps considerably with the synchronous increases in activity seen in the panneuronal line in segments A7-A5 that characterize the interwave phase.
source: Instead, A26f activity overlaps considerably with the synchronous increases in activity seen in the panneuronal line in segments A7-A5 that characterize the interwave phase (Figure 4C; see 'Discussion').
evidence: Supported by temporal analysis of dual-color calcium imaging data.

claim: The activity of A26f segmental homologs is highly correlated, unlike pan-neuronal activity.
source: Consistent with their synchronized activity, the activity of A26f segmental homologs is highly correlated, unlike pan-neuronal activity (Figure 4E).
evidence: Supported by cross-correlation analysis of calcium imaging data.

claim: The synchronous peak of A26f neurons is 'bookended' by the peaks in A31c activity of neighboring segments.
source: We found that the synchronous peak of A26f neurons is 'bookended' by the peaks in A31c activity of neighboring segments (Figure 4F).
evidence: Supported by simultaneous calcium imaging of A31c and A26f neurons.

claim: The alternating activity pattern between A31c and A26f is consistent with the inhibitory nature of the A31c-A26f synapses.
source: This alternating activity pattern between A31c and A26f is consistent with the inhibitory nature of the A31c-A26f synapses and suggests these cell types might be involved in determining the duration of the interwave phase.
evidence: Based on temporal relationship of activity patterns and known GABAergic identity of A31c.

claim: Activation of A26f neurons reduces the contraction amplitude of the LT2 muscle during forward crawling.
source: Activation of the A26f neurons reduced the contraction amplitude of the LT2 muscle, while the contraction of the VL2 muscle was almost unchanged (Figure 5C and D and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by optogenetic activation experiments combined with muscle imaging in sideways preparation.

claim: Activation of A31c neurons is sufficient to activate the LT muscles.
source: The stimulation caused the contraction of LT muscles in all visualized abdominal neuromeres (A3-A8; Figure 5G), causing a reduction in the minimum length of the LT2 muscle (Figure 5H). These results suggest that activation of A31c neurons is sufficient to activate the LT muscles.
evidence: Supported by optogenetic activation experiments in fillet preparation showing LT muscle contraction.

claim: Optogenetic silencing of A26f neurons increases the contraction of LT2 muscles.
source: We found that the minimum length of muscle LT2 decreased after optogenetic silencing of A26f, suggesting increased levels of contraction (Figure 6A and B).
evidence: Supported by optogenetic silencing experiments combined with muscle imaging.

claim: Optogenetic silencing of A31c neurons increases the minimum length of LT2 muscles during forward cycles.
source: We found that after optogenetic silencing the minimum length of the LT2 muscle in segment A5 was increased during forward cycles (Figure 6A and B).
evidence: Supported by optogenetic silencing experiments combined with muscle imaging.

claim: The activity of A26f and A31c neurons is necessary for the appropriate contractions of LT muscles observed during locomotor cycles.
source: These results reveal that the activity of A26f and A31c neurons is necessary for the appropriate contractions of LT muscles observed during locomotor cycles.
evidence: Supported by optogenetic silencing experiments showing altered LT muscle contractions.

claim: Activation of A26f neurons decreases the interwave phase duration during free crawling.
source: By analyzing the kinematics, we confirmed that the interwave phase and the total stride duration were both significantly decreased during the optogenetic activation (Figure 7C and C').
evidence: Supported by optogenetic activation experiments during free crawling with kinematic analysis.

claim: Activation of A26f neurons increases crawling speed.
source: Consistent with these results, the speed of crawling was significantly increased (Figure 7C'').
evidence: Supported by optogenetic activation experiments during free crawling with speed measurements.

claim: Inhibiting A26f neurons increases the interwave duration and stride duration.
source: We found that inhibiting the A26f neurons increased the interwave duration and stride duration but had no significant effect on the wave duration (Figure 7D and D' and Figure 7—figure supplement 1C), resulting in decreased speeds (Figure 7D'').
evidence: Supported by optogenetic inhibition experiments during free crawling with kinematic analysis.

claim: A26f neurons are involved in regulating the speed of locomotion by modulating the contraction of LT muscles.
source: Combined with our previous analyses, these results indicate that the A26f neurons are involved in regulating the speed of locomotion by modulating the contraction of LT muscles.
evidence: Supported by combined results from muscle imaging and behavioral optogenetic experiments.

claim: Activation of A31c neurons increases the interwave duration and stride duration.
source: During the activation of A31c neurons, the interwave duration and the stride duration were significantly increased, while no significant difference was found in the wave duration (Figure 7E and E' and Figure 7—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: Supported by optogenetic activation experiments during free crawling with kinematic analysis.

claim: The effects of A31c activation on crawling kinematics are consistent with those observed during the inhibition of A26f neurons.
source: These effects are consistent with those observed during the inhibition of A26f neurons (Figure 7D and D' and Figure 7—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Supported by comparison of optogenetic manipulation results for A31c and A26f.

claim: Inhibition of A31c neurons does not induce defects in crawling kinematics.
source: On the other hand, the inhibition of A31c neurons, which we achieved by expressing GtACR1 in A31c neurons using the A31c-sp driver line, did not induce defects in crawling kinematics (Figure 7F–F'' and Figure 7—figure supplement 1G and H).
evidence: Supported by optogenetic inhibition experiments during free crawling showing no significant kinematic changes.

claim: Additional cell types to A31c could set the level and timing of activity in A26f and therefore the speed of locomotion.
source: This implies that additional cell types to A31c could set the level and timing of activity in A26f and therefore the speed of locomotion.
evidence: Inferred from the lack of effect of A31c inhibition on crawling kinematics.

claim: The Drosophila larva uses a strategy to primarily vary the phase between consecutive peristaltic waves for speed regulation.
source: We used the Drosophila larva as a model and found that this animal uses a strategy to primarily vary the phase between consecutive peristaltic waves for speed regulation.
evidence: Supported by kinematic analysis showing differential modulation of interwave vs. wave phase with speed.

claim: The larva modulates the amplitude and duration of the contraction of the LT muscles to implement speed regulation.
source: To implement this strategy, the larva modulates the amplitude and duration of the contraction of the LT muscles that are perpendicular to the crawling direction, which contract synchronously along the anterior-posterior axis before the onset of the peristaltic wave.
evidence: Supported by muscle imaging data showing correlation between LT muscle contraction parameters and interwave phase duration.

claim: A31c neurons receive shared descending input.
source: Connectivity analysis further revealed that A31c neurons receive shared descending input and synapse onto ascending neurons and local neurons, including A26f.
evidence: Supported by EM connectomics analysis showing descending neuron S10 as major input to A31c across segments.

claim: A31c neurons synapse onto ascending neurons and local neurons, including A26f.
source: Connectivity analysis further revealed that A31c neurons receive shared descending input and synapse onto ascending neurons and local neurons, including A26f.
evidence: Supported by EM connectomics analysis showing A31c postsynaptic partners including A26f and ascending neurons like A19f.

claim: A26f and A31c neurons are involved in modulating the activity of the LT muscles and thus the interwave duration and speed.
source: These neurons are involved in modulating the activity of the LT muscles and thus the interwave duration and speed.
evidence: Supported by combined results from optogenetic manipulation, muscle imaging, and behavioral analysis.

claim: The speed of Drosophila larval crawling is determined more by stride frequency than stride length.
source: We found that, similar to previous findings, the speed of Drosophila larval crawling is determined more so by stride frequency than stride length (Frigon et al., 2014; Grillner et al., 1979; Jacobson and Hollyday, 1982; Nirody et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis of crawling data and cited previous work in other species.

claim: Similar to limbed animals, the two constituent phases of a locomotor cycle in Drosophila larvae vary differentially with speed.
source: Furthermore, similar to limbed animals including mammals and other insects, the two constituent phases of a locomotor cycle vary differentially with speed, with the interwave phase varying more than the wave phase.
evidence: Supported by kinematic analysis showing differential modulation of phases and comparison with cited literature on limbed locomotion.

claim: The similarity between the dynamics of locomotion between limbed and axial locomotion could be indicative of the kinematic constraints of each type of movement.
source: This similarity between the dynamics of locomotion between limbed and axial locomotion could be indicative of the kinematic constraints of each type of movement.
evidence: Speculative interpretation based on observed similarities between larval and limbed locomotion.

claim: The relative invariance of the duration of the swing phase in limbed locomotion suggests that the rotational inertia of swinging limbs may be an important limiting factor.
source: In both cases, the relative invariance of the duration of this phase suggests that the rotational inertia of swinging limbs may be an important limiting factor in limbed locomotion (Kilbourne, 2013a; Kilbourne and Hoffman, 2013b; Kilbourne and Hoffman, 2015; Rocha‐Barbosa et al., 2005).
evidence: Speculative interpretation based on cited literature about limbed locomotion mechanics.

claim: The relative invariance of the peristaltic wave phase in the Drosophila larva suggests a similar constraint on its motor system.
source: The relative invariance of the peristaltic wave phase in the Drosophila larva suggests a similar constraint on the its motor system.
evidence: Speculative interpretation based on observed wave phase invariance and comparison with limbed locomotion.

claim: The transverse muscles may be an evolutionary adaptation, with an additional set of neurons having developed to control them.
source: Furthermore, the transverse muscles, and therefore its contractions during the interwave phase, may be an evolutionary adaptation, with an additional set of neurons having developed to control them.
evidence: Speculative interpretation based on evolutionary considerations and observed neural control.

claim: The last common ancestor to all bilaterians is thought to have only had circular and longitudinal muscles.
source: Consistent with this hypothesis, the last common ancestor to all bilaterians, the so-called 'Urbilaterian,' is thought to have only had circular and longitudinal muscles (Cannon et al., 2016), and transverse muscles have only been identified in the larvae of some other species of Diptera (e.g., Tribolium castaneum, Schultheis et al., 2019; Galleria mellonella, Emery et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by cited evolutionary and comparative studies.

claim: Transverse muscles have only been identified in the larvae of some species of Diptera.
source: Consistent with this hypothesis, the last common ancestor to all bilaterians, the so-called 'Urbilaterian,' is thought to have only had circular and longitudinal muscles (Cannon et al., 2016), and transverse muscles have only been identified in the larvae of some other species of Diptera (e.g., Tribolium castaneum, Schultheis et al., 2019; Galleria mellonella, Emery et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by cited comparative studies in other insect species.

claim: The transverse muscles are under independent neuromodulatory control.
source: Furthermore, the transverse muscles are under independent neuromodulatory control (Elliott et al., 2021), and their motor neurons are innervated by a distinct set of interneurons (Zwart et al., 2016; Kohsaka et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by cited previous work on neuromodulation and neural circuits.

claim: The motor neurons of transverse muscles are innervated by a distinct set of interneurons.
source: Furthermore, the transverse muscles are under independent neuromodulatory control (Elliott et al., 2021), and their motor neurons are innervated by a distinct set of interneurons (Zwart et al., 2016; Kohsaka et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by cited previous work on neural circuits.

claim: The mesencephalic locomotor region (MLR) has been identified in all vertebrate species studied to date as an important control center for locomotion speed.
source: The mesencephalic locomotor region (MLR), which projects to reticulospinal neurons that in turn innervate spinal circuits, has been identified in all vertebrate species studied to date as an important control center (Ryczko et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by cited review of vertebrate locomotion control.

claim: Increasingly intense stimulation of the MLR causes increases in the speed of locomotion, with accompanying gait transitions.
source: Increasingly intense stimulation of the MLR causes increases in the speed of locomotion, with accompanying gait transitions (Atsuta et al., 1990; Grillner, 1985; Shik et al., 1966; Shik and Orlovsky, 1976; Skinner and Garcia-Rill, 1984).
evidence: Supported by cited experimental studies on MLR stimulation.

claim: In a range of species, descending projecting excitatory neurons have been shown to drive the rhythm of locomotion.
source: In a range of species, descending projecting excitatory neurons have been shown to drive the rhythm of locomotion (Berg et al., 2018; Caggiano et al., 2018; Capelli et al., 2017; Friesen and Kristan, 2007; Gatto and Goulding, 2018; Josset et al., 2018; Roberts et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by cited studies across multiple species.

claim: In mice, excitatory neurons are necessary and sufficient for rhythm generation in the spinal cord.
source: In mice, studies using optogenetics have shown that excitatory neurons are necessary and sufficient for rhythm generation (Hägglund et al., 2010; Hägglund et al., 2013), with studies ongoing to uncover the precise identity of the rhythm generators (Kiehn, 2016).
evidence: Supported by cited optogenetic studies in mice.

claim: Zebrafish have different central modules corresponding to fast, intermediate, and slow locomotion that are selectively recruited.
source: Zebrafish, which use axial locomotion to move, have different central modules corresponding in adults to fast, intermediate, and slow locomotion that are selectively recruited to command the motor pools specific for different speeds (Ampatzis et al., 2013; Ampatzis et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by cited studies on zebrafish locomotion circuits.

claim: Swimming animals modulate their undulatory frequency by controlling the intersegmental lag, which is linearly scaled with the locomotor cycle duration.
source: Swimming animals modulate their undulatory frequency by controlling the intersegmental lag, which is linearly scaled with the locomotor cycle duration (Grillner, 1974).
evidence: Supported by cited work on swimming locomotion.

claim: Limbed animals change the frequency of walking by varying the stance phase but keeping the swing phase almost unchanged.
source: On the other hand, limbed animals change the frequency of walking by varying the locomotor cycle differentially: the stance phase is varied, but the swing phase is almost unchanged, even as animals switch to different gaits. This holds true for animals ranging from insects and tardigrades to mammals (Boije and Kullander, 2018; Frigon et al., 2014; Grillner et al., 1979; Jacobson and Hollyday, 1982; Nirody et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by cited studies across multiple species with limbed locomotion.

claim: Reciprocal inhibition within the spinal cord is thought to underlie the generation of alternation during locomotion.
source: One of the simplest circuit designs for rhythm generation, the 'half-center oscillator,' relies on reciprocal inhibition to generate alternating patterns of activity (Marder and Bucher, 2001), and reciprocal inhibition within the spinal cord is thought to underlie the generation of alternation during locomotion (Deliagina and Orlovsky, 1980; Geertsen et al., 2011; Pratt and Jordan, 1987).
evidence: Supported by cited theoretical and experimental work on locomotor circuits.

claim: Inhibitory neurons shape the rhythms of neural activity on different timescales in systems from crustacean stomatogastric ganglion to vertebrate cortical circuits.
source: Indeed, inhibitory neurons shape the rhythms of neural activity on different timescales in systems from crustacean stomatogastric ganglion to vertebrate cortical circuits (Cardin, 2019; Marder and Bucher, 2001).
evidence: Supported by cited reviews on inhibitory circuit function.

claim: In cats, the extensor muscles are mainly activated during the stance phase, while the flexor muscles are mainly activated in the swing phase.
source: For instance, in cats, the extensor muscles are mainly activated during the stance phase, while the flexor muscles are mainly activated in the swing phase (Engberg and Lundberg, 1969); similarly, we found that the fruit fly larva contracts its transverse muscles during the interwave phase, and its longitudinal muscles during the wave phase.
evidence: Supported by cited work on cat locomotion and comparison with larval data.

claim: The inhibitory neural circuit motif underlying the generation of the asymmetry of the two constituent phases of locomotion could be conserved between species.
source: These parallels may be mirrored within the neural circuitry mediating these muscle contractions. While the detailed implementation will obviously differ, the inhibitory neural circuit motif underlying the generation of the asymmetry of the two constituent phases of locomotion could therefore be conserved between species.
evidence: Speculative interpretation based on observed parallels between larval and limbed locomotion.

claim: Descending input has the potential to shape the activity of the speed modulation circuit through A31c neurons.
source: Our EM connectomics results also show that descending input has the potential to shape the activity of the speed modulation circuit. A31c receives strong synaptic input from descending neurons (e.g., S10 and T19x make up 32% of total input of A31cs in segments A2 and A3); the levels and timing of activity in A31c could therefore be modulated by descending cell types, which in turn could affect the activity of A26f and therefore the speed of crawling.
evidence: Supported by EM connectomics data showing descending inputs to A31c.

claim: Descending input to A31c could act to synchronize the activity of A31c across abdominal segments.
source: It is also possible that this descending input acts to synchronize the activity of A31c across abdominal segments.
evidence: Speculative interpretation based on shared descending input pattern.

claim: Ascending projections postsynaptic to A31c could be involved in relaying the state of the motor network to higher brain centers.
source: Moreover, there are several cell types postsynaptic to A31c that send ascending projections from the VNC to thoracic and subesophageal segments (VNC-IN, A19f). These could be involved in relaying the state of the motor network, for example, to provide higher brain centers with information on the current phase of the locomotor cycle or the intended speed of locomotion.
evidence: Speculative interpretation based on connectivity patterns of A31c postsynaptic partners.

claim: Physically restricted larvae and the isolated CNS have long cycle periods (2–20 s), presumably due to aberrant or absent input from sensory neurons.
source: However, physically restricted larvae and the isolated CNS have long cycle periods (2–20 s), presumably due to aberrant or absent input from sensory neurons (Caldwell et al., 2003; Hughes and Thomas, 2007; Schützler et al., 2019; Zarin et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by cited previous work on restricted preparations and inference about sensory input.

claim: The normal range of cycle periods in freely crawling larvae is 0.6–2 s.
source: How the larva varies locomotion in crawling within the normal range of cycle periods (0.6–2 s) is therefore not understood.
evidence: Stated as background information defining the normal range.

claim: The intersegmental lag between the contraction of adjacent segments during the peristaltic wave scales with the cycle period in the intact animal and the isolated CNS.
source: It has been shown that the lag between the contraction of adjacent segments during the peristaltic wave (intersegmental lag) scales with the cycle period in the intact animal and the isolated CNS (Heckscher et al., 2012; Lemon et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by cited previous work.

claim: Crawling speed correlates with stride period more than stride length in mildly physically restrained first-instar larvae.
source: A previous study in mildly physically restrained first-instar larvae showed that crawling speed correlates with stride period more than stride length (Heckscher et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by cited previous work.

claim: Longitudinal muscles in the posterior-most segments (VL4 and DO1 in A6 and A7) contract during the interwave phase.
source: Third, the longitudinal muscles in the posterior-most segments (VL4 and DO1 in A6 and A7 in Figure 1—figure supplement 1G') contract during the interwave phase (see 'Discussion').
evidence: Supported by side-view muscle imaging data.

claim: The axon of A26f in neuromere A5 extends four neuromeres from A6 neuromere to A3 neuromere.
source: As a representative example, the axon of A26f in neuromere A5 extends four neuromeres from A6 neuromere to A3 neuromere (Figure 4B).
evidence: Supported by morphological analysis from confocal imaging and EM reconstruction.

claim: A26f neurons can exhibit one or several peaks at the initiation phase of the fictive forward wave.
source: A26f neurons can exhibit one or several peaks at the initiation phase of the FW (Figure 4C and D).
evidence: Supported by calcium imaging data showing variable peak patterns.

claim: A26f neurons have synaptic input sites dorsally near the midline and synaptic output sites near the DL tract.
source: A26f neurons have synaptic input sites dorsally near the midline and synaptic output sites near the DL tract (Figure 4B).
evidence: Supported by synaptic marker imaging showing spatial distribution of pre- and postsynaptic sites.

claim: A31c neurons have synaptic input sites along the dorsolateral (DL) tract and synaptic output sites mainly positioned dorsally near the midline.
source: The synaptic input sites are located along the dorsolateral (DL) tract (Landgraf et al., 2003), while the synaptic output sites are mainly positioned dorsally near the midline (Figure 2A and B).
evidence: Supported by synaptic marker imaging and EM reconstruction showing spatial distribution of synapses.

claim: A31c neurons project dorsally by approximately one neuromere, mostly to the anterior.
source: The neurites project dorsally by approximately one neuromere, mostly to the anterior (Figure 2A).
evidence: Supported by morphological analysis from EM reconstruction and genetic labeling.

claim: A26f neurons receive synaptic inputs from the ascending cell type A19f.
source: A26f neurons also receive synaptic inputs from the ascending cell type A19f, one of the top postsynaptic partners of A31c neurons (Jonaitis, 2020).
evidence: Supported by EM connectomics analysis and cited work.

claim: Most A31c-sp+ cells in the brain are positive to Deadpan (dpn), a marker for neuroblast.
source: However, the majority of A31c-sp+ cells in the brain are positive to Deadpan (dpn) (Figure 7—figure supplement 2D), a marker for neuroblast (Doe, 2017), and the terminals of A31c-sp+ cells in the brain lack synapse-like morphology, suggesting that most A31c-sp+ cells in the brain are not mature neurons.
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data showing dpn expression and morphological analysis.
